meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The essence of formulating strategy is relating a company to its environment'?
meta.ogDescription: The line is Porter's, opening Chapter 1 of Competitive Strategy (1980), p. 3 — but he wrote "formulating competitive strategy." Quote sites dropped a word.

answer.label: Not quite — Porter wrote “formulating competitive strategy”
answer.authorDates: b. 1947 · Harvard Business School economist · written 1980
answer.sourceLine: The author is right and the page reference is right: this is the opening sentence of Chapter 1 of Competitive Strategy (The Free Press, New York, 1980), on p. 3. But the sentence Porter actually printed reads “The essence of formulating competitive strategy is relating a company to its environment” — the version in circulation has lost the one adjective the whole chapter is built on.

trail: 1979 — Porter publishes “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” in the March–April Harvard Business Review ↗. Its opening sentence is a close cousin of this one: “The essence of strategy formulation is coping with competition.”

1980 — Competitive Strategy: Techniques for Analyzing Industries and Competitors is published by The Free Press in New York (Open Library edition record ↗). Its Chapter 1, “The Structural Analysis of Industries,” begins on p. 3 with the sentence at issue.

Checked against the book — a full-text search of Competitive Strategy returns exactly one sentence beginning “The essence of formulating,” and it contains the word competitive. Anyone can confirm the printed wording in one click: the Open Library record for the 1980 Free Press edition ↗ prints its First Sentence field as “The essence of formulating competitive strategy is relating a company to its environment.”

Today — Wikiquote ↗ carries the shortened wording with the correct p. 3 citation, and the aggregator layer displays the same wording with the same citation. Quote Investigator has not examined this line; there is nothing to examine — the source was never in doubt, only the transcription.
source.excerptNote: That is the sentence as printed — the first line of Chapter 1, checked against the book’s own text. The version in circulation is identical apart from the word competitive. Because Competitive Strategy is still in copyright, only this one sentence is reproduced here; the surrounding paragraph goes on to narrow “environment” to the industry the firm competes in.

author.metaLine: b. 1947 · Harvard Business School economist · strategy theorist
author.bio: Michael Eugene Porter, born 23 May 1947, is the Harvard Business School economist who turned “strategy” from a boardroom mood into something you could diagram. His 1979 Harvard Business Review article “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” and his 1980 book Competitive Strategy introduced the five-forces model of industry structure, still a standard opening framework in MBA strategy teaching. He was appointed Bishop William Lawrence University Professor at Harvard in 2000.

misattribution.heading: Where the word went
misattribution.intro: Nobody has pinned this line on the wrong person. The drift is subtler and, for a strategy quotation, funnier: the missing word is the one Porter’s entire book is about.

Porter opened “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy” in the March–April 1979 Harvard Business Review ↗ with a different ‘essence’ line: “The essence of strategy formulation is coping with competition.” Two similar openers a year apart, and quotation lists routinely merge them.

misattribution.truthLine: Porter wrote it, in the place everyone says he did — the first sentence of Chapter 1 of Competitive Strategy (The Free Press, New York, 1980), p. 3. It just reads “The essence of formulating competitive strategy is relating a company to its environment.” Open Library prints that sentence as the book’s first sentence ↗.

context.heading: Why the missing word matters
lead: Dropping “competitive” sounds like housekeeping. It is not. The sentence is the first line of a chapter titled “The Structural Analysis of Industries,” and Porter’s next move is to narrow “environment” hard: the relevant environment is broad, he concedes, encompassing social as well as economic forces — but the key aspect of it is the industry the firm competes in. That narrowing is the argument. It is what produces the five forces.

Read without the adjective, the line becomes the blandest possible claim: companies should pay attention to their surroundings. Nobody has ever disagreed with that. Read as written, it is a much sharper bet — that the part of the environment worth modelling is the competitive structure of your industry, and that the rest is significant mainly in a relative sense, because outside forces tend to hit every firm in the industry at once.
context.detailsSummary: Porter’s two ‘essence’ openers, one year apart
detailsBody: Porter opened two founding texts with an “essence” sentence, and they are easy to blend. The Harvard Business Review article of March–April 1979, “How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy,” begins: “The essence of strategy formulation is coping with competition.” The book that followed in 1980 begins: “The essence of formulating competitive strategy is relating a company to its environment.”

Same author, same idea, different sentences — and both get quoted as though there were only one. If you are citing the line about the environment, it is the book; if you are citing the line about coping with competition, it is the article.
context.pull: One adjective is doing the work of an entire framework.

sourcesVerified.claim: Competitive Strategy (The Free Press, 1980) opens Chapter 1, "The Structural Analysis of Industries", on p. 3 with the sentence "The essence of formulating competitive strategy is relating a company to its environment." The copyright page names one claimant — it reads "Copyright © 1980 by The Free Press" (with "New introduction copyright © 1998 by The Free Press") and "First Free Press Edition 1980", with Porter nowhere named as a rights holder; the table of contents lists Chapter 1 at p. 3. Verified by downloading the full text and extracting it twice (with and without layout preservation); the phrase "essence of formulating" occurs exactly once in the book.
